{{Group theory sidebar |Basics}}

In [[group theory]], an area of [[mathematics]], an '''infinite group''' is a [[group (mathematics)|group]] whose [[forgetful functor|underlying set]] contains [[infinite set|infinitely many]] [[element (mathematics)|element]]s. In other words, it is a group of infinite [[Order (group theory)|order]]. The structure of infinite groups is often a question of [[mathematical analysis]] of the [[asymptotic]]s of how various invariants grow relative to a generating set, or how a group [[group action|acts]] on a [[topological space|topological]] or [[measure space]]. In contrast, the structure of [[finite group]]s is determined largely by methods of [[abstract algebra]].

== Examples ==
* ('''Z''', +), the group of [[Integer|integers]] with addition is infinite, as is ('''Q''', +) the group of [[Rational number|rational numbers]] with addition
* Non-discrete [[Lie group]]s are infinite. For example, ('''R''', +), the group of [[Real number|real numbers]] with addition is an infinite group
* The [[general linear group]] of order ''n'' > 0 over an infinite [[Field (mathematics)|field]] is infinite
* The [[Infinite dihedral group]]
* The [[Tarski monster group]]
* The [[Prüfer group|Prüfer p-group]]
* A [[free group]]
* [[SL(2,Z)]]
* [[Amenable group]]s
* [[Thompson groups]]
* [[Grigorchuk group]]
* [[Lamplighter group]]s

== Torsion ==
An infinite group is called a [[torsion group]] if every element has finite order. Examples include the Prüfer ''p''-group and certain Burnside groups. In contrast, a group is torsion-free if no non-identity element has finite order, such as <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> or free groups.

== Structure and classification ==
Many infinite groups are given in terms of a set of generators and relations.  For example, a [[free group]] is a group on a set of generators with no relations, whereas a [[braid group]] is a group on generators <math>g_i</math>, where <math>i</math> is an integer in <math>[0,n]</math>, with relations <math>g_i g_{i+1} g_i = g_{i+1} g_i g_{i+1}</math> and <math>g_ig_j=g_jg_i</math> if <math>|i-j|>1</math>.

Infinite groups can be finitely generated, such as <math>\mathbb Z</math> or <math>\operatorname{SL}(n,\mathbb Z)</math>, or infinitely generated such as <math>(\mathbb Q,+)</math> or any [[Lie group]]; finitely presented such as any free group (on a finite set of generators) or braid groups. Groups may also be infinitely presented, etc.

An infinite group may be [[residually finite]], meaning that every element is non-trivial in some finite quotient. Many groups, like <math>\operatorname{SL}(n,\mathbb Z)</math>, are residually finite; whereas others like the [[Tarski monster group]]s, are not.

Many infinite groups are [[linear group]]s, meaning that they have a faithful representation on a finite-dimensional vector space. This includes groups like <math>\operatorname{SL}(n,\mathbb Z)</math> and every [[classical group]] (via its [[adjoint representation]]), and every finitely-generated torsion-free nilpotent group, by [[Malcev's theorem]], but not groups like the [[metaplectic group]].

Some infinite groups are [[simple group|simple]], such as the [[Thompson groups]].

== Asymptotics ==
An infinite group equipped with a generating set <math>\{\gamma_i \mid i \in I\}</math> inherits a natural metric structure via the [[word metric]]. This is the unique left-invariant distance function such that <math>d(\gamma_i, e) = d(\gamma_i^{-1}, e) = 1</math> for each generator <math>\gamma_i</math>, and distances extend by minimal word length. The resulting metric space is locally a [[discrete topological space]], but its large-scale geometry exhibits meaningful structure. For instance, the volume of a ball of radius <math>r</math> (i.e., the number of group elements expressible using at most <math>r</math> generators) grows in a way that reflects intrinsic properties of the group—such as polynomial growth in [[nilpotent group]]s or exponential growth in [[free group]]s.<ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Gerl |editor-first=Martin R. |editor2-last=Kosniowski |editor2-first=Czes |title=Geometric Group Theory, Volume 2 |series=London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series |volume=182 |url=https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/492.pdf |first=Mikhael |last=Gromov |author-link=Mikhael Gromov (mathematician) |year=1993 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |pages=1–295 |isbn=978-0521446808}}</ref>

A finitely generated group has polynomial growth if and only if it is [[virtually nilpotent]], and that the group's large-scale geometry can often be understood via its [[asymptotic cone]]—a kind of limiting metric space that captures the group's behavior "at infinity".

Many other aspects of infinite groups can be expressed in terms of the word metric, such as [[amenable group|amenability]]: a group is ''not'' amenable, if and only if there exist constants <math>d</math> and <math>C</math> such that, for every finite subset <math>S</math>, <math>|S|\le C |\partial_d S|</math>, where <math>\partial_d S</math> is the set of points within a distance <math>d</math> of any element of <math>S</math>.
